items.note: Paramāras traditionally regarded as Agnikula, born of the yajña-kuṇḍa of sage Vashishta; quotes Dasharatha Sharma that only the Paramāras are the true Agnikula clan (secondary overview, not specific to Udaypur).
Padmagupta's Navasāhasāṅkacarita, composed in Sindhurāja's time, places the Paramāra origin at Arbudāchala (Mount Abu), tapo-land of Vasishtha.
Vasishtha's fire-pit offering produced the Chauhans, Pariharas, Paramāras and Solankis; the paper adds that specific information on the four dynasties is not available.
Malwa as original residence of the Paramāras, capitals Ujjain and Dhārā, and the extent of the kingdom including parts of Bhilsa (citing Ganguly 2013).
Both the Udaipur Praśasti and the Navasāhasāṅkacarita mention Upendra as the first great Paramāra king.
Udaipur record lists Upendra, then Vairisiṃha, Siyaka and Vākpati Muñja; the paper notes some names are not clearly recorded and other rulers may have intervened.
Verse 10 of the Udaipur Praśasti, on the eyes of the Avanti princesses, taken as showing Vākpati I's dominion over the area.
Vākpati Muñja (973-995) as adopted son of Siyaka, his wars against the Kalachuri and Chalukya king Tailapa.
Vākpati as patron of poets and scholars; Padmagupta and Dhananjaya lived in his state.
Sindhurāja succeeds Muñja, takes the titles Nārāyaṇa and Sahasāṅka; father of Bhoja; known from Padmagupta's Navasāhasāṅkacarita and Bhoja's stone inscriptions.
Siyaka's north-west campaign against the Hun princes, per the Navasāhasāṅkacarita; wars with the Huns continued to the end of the tenth century.
Bhoja as ninth Paramāra king, temple builder in Malwa, patron of scholars and author said to have written about 84 books.
Sanskrit verse on Dhārā and Sarasvatī while Bhoja lives, with the paper's English meaning: pandits and scholars honoured at his court.
items.gloss: Today Dhārā has a firm support, Sarasvatī has a prop; all the learned are adorned, while Bhoja rules on earth.

items.note: Bhoja's Banswara and Betama records of Samvat 1076 (1020): land gift to a Brahmin and donations after the Konkan victory.
Udaipur Praśasti on Bhoja's victory over Indraratha while fighting the Solanki Jayasiṃha; wars with Lāṭa and with Muslims.
Paramāra decline: Yadava invasion from the south, internal wars, and Muslim invasions of the lower eastern border of Malwa.
Visaladeva's 1243 invasion of Malwa; the Paramāra empire destroyed by frequent wars with neighbouring kings.
